posts.title: Inside Invoke-KqlPS
posts.summary: Why I built a KQL interpreter in PowerShell, what subset it supports today, and how it anchors the rest of the lab.

sections.heading: Why build a local KQL harness at all
paragraphs: The problem was simple: I wanted a place to practice hunting patterns against realistic Sentinel-shaped data without needing a live tenant, ingest budget, or demo workspace every time I wanted to test an idea.

That led to `Invoke-KqlPS.ps1`, a scoped Kusto Query Language interpreter in pure PowerShell. It loads tables from a local SQLite database whose schema mirrors the Microsoft Sentinel / Log Analytics table shapes I care about, keeps rows in memory as PowerShell objects, and treats each tabular operator as a function that takes a table and returns a new table. The pipe stays the mental model all the way through.

The module was never meant to be "all of KQL." The useful target was the subset that shows up constantly in daily SOC work: `where`, `project`, `extend`, `summarize`, `distinct`, `union`, several join kinds, `parse with`, and `mv-expand`, plus the scalar functions you reach for while cleaning data or building pivots.

sections.heading: What the current interpreter actually covers
paragraphs: The supported surface is intentionally honest and written down in the module header. On the tabular side, the interpreter handles:

• `take`, `limit`, `top` • `where` • `project`, `project-keep`, `project-rename`, `project-away` • `extend` • `summarize ... by ...` • `order by` / `sort by` • `distinct` • `union` • `join kind=inner|leftouter|leftanti|innerunique` • `parse with` • `mv-expand` • pass-through handling for `materialize`, `getschema`, and `render`

On the scalar side, it supports the functions I wanted available while teaching or validating hunts: time helpers like `ago()` and `now()`, converters like `tostring()` and `toint()`, string helpers like `startswith`, `contains`, and `split`, and collection helpers like `make_set`, `make_list`, `array_length`, and `array_index_of`.

Just as important, the out-of-scope list is explicit. `mv-apply`, `evaluate bag_unpack`, `series_*`, parameterized user-defined functions, and external tables are not quietly half-implemented. They raise a clear error so the failure mode is "you hit an unsupported feature" instead of "you got a plausible-looking but wrong result."

sections.heading: The reproducibility trick that made the lab usable
paragraphs: One design detail matters more than it sounds: the module freezes the "current time" anchor when the context is created.

That means `ago()` and `now()` are reproducible against the static sample data. The browser lab and the PowerShell lab both depend on that idea. If the reference clock drifted with the user's system clock, training queries would keep getting weirder as the bundled data aged. Freezing the reference time lets the dataset stay static while the exercises still behave like they're running against a fresh window.
That small constraint is why the same query examples can be taught in the guide, graded in the practice harness, and validated in the browser engine without everyone getting different answers.

sections.heading: Why SQLite sits underneath it
paragraphs: SQLite is the storage layer, not the query language. The companion `Build-KqlLabDb.ps1` script stages CSV log samples into tables that match the production-style schema, and `Import-KqlLabCsv.ps1` handles the type coercion.
That split matters:

• SQLite gives me a portable local store. • PowerShell gives me a place to model KQL semantics directly. • The sample tables keep the field names and data shapes familiar enough that a hunt can move from the lab into Sentinel or ADX with minimal translation.
The browser lab later ports the same mental model into JavaScript and WASM SQLite, but the PowerShell version is the original reference implementation.

sections.heading: Where this fits in the rest of the site
paragraphs: `Invoke-KqlPS` is not an isolated script. It is the anchor point for a bigger chain:
• the local lab database builder • the KQL guide and examples • the browser playground • the 30-question practice harness • the validation matrix that keeps the browser port honest
That is the part I care about most. The goal was never just to write a parser. It was to build a practice environment where the query, the data, the lesson, and the grading path all line up.

If you want to poke at the browser side of the same idea, start with the [KQL Playground](/kql/) and [KQL Practice](/lab/practice/). If you want the PowerShell module inventory, the [Scripts page](/scripts/) is the map.

posts.title: MITRE Crosswalks in the Lab
posts.summary: How the local ATT&CK data, CVE-to-technique mappings, and KQL tooling fit together in one offline-friendly workflow.

sections.heading: The problem I wanted to solve
paragraphs: I did not want ATT&CK living in my tooling as a poster on the wall.

The useful version of ATT&CK is the one that can sit next to the things an analyst is already doing: checking whether a technique is relevant, seeing what data sources it expects, comparing it with recent CVEs, and turning that into a query or triage path without opening six tabs.
That is the job of the MITRE crosswalk pieces in this repo.

sections.heading: The local explorer starts with the full STIX bundle
paragraphs: `MitreAttackExplorer.ps1` downloads the Enterprise ATT&CK STIX bundle, parses it, and loads the useful pieces into the same SQLite database used by the rest of the SOC Dashboard tooling.
The ingest path stores:
• tactics • techniques and sub-techniques • intrusion sets • software • mitigations • relationships

The important design choice is that ATT&CK data is cached locally after the first run. That keeps the tool fast, user-level, and workable in environments where the interesting part of the day is analysis rather than waiting on a remote dependency.

For a while there was a browser version of the explorer on this site too. It shipped a slimmed static dataset so the public side stayed usable without a backend. I ended up pulling it down - the local dashboard explorer is where that work actually lives, and keeping two copies honest was more upkeep than it was worth.

sections.heading: CVE-to-ATT&CK mapping is intentionally a separate layer
paragraphs: The ATT&CK bundle alone answers "what is this technique?" It does not answer "which current vulnerabilities line up with the behavior I care about?"

That is why `Update-CveAttackMap.ps1` exists as a separate import step. It reads a CSV with `CveId` and `TechniqueId` columns, plus optional `Source`, `Confidence`, and `Mapping` fields, then loads those rows into the database as a first-class lookup table.
Separating the mapping layer from the ATT&CK ingest keeps a few good things true:

1. Multiple mapping sources can coexist. 2. Analyst-curated mappings are not flattened into someone else's feed. 3. The explorer and the patching views can show confidence and provenance, instead of pretending every mapping is equally authoritative.
The script header even calls out the intended mapping sources: the Center for Threat-Informed Defense mappings, NVD/CWE-derived bridges, and analyst-curated entries from local investigations.

sections.heading: Why this matters in practice
paragraphs: A local crosswalk turns three separate questions into one working loop:
• What technique is this adversary behavior pointing at? • What data source should see it? • Which current CVEs or products make that technique more urgent right now?
That is the connective tissue between the ATT&CK explorer, the CVE/KEV/EPSS browser, and the KQL tooling.

If a technique shows up repeatedly in ATT&CK-oriented research, and the related products are present in KEV with strong EPSS or ransomware linkage, that should change the order in which I write detections, validate log coverage, or bug a team about patching.
The repo already leans into that connection:

• the ATT&CK explorer keeps tactic / platform / relationship context close • the CVE browser already ships KEV and EPSS together • the KQL templates and practice surfaces provide a place to turn the framework view into an actual hunt

sections.heading: Why keep it offline-friendly
paragraphs: One theme across this site is that the interesting part should survive without a constant live dependency.

That is true for the KQL engine, and it is also true here. The ATT&CK bundle can be cached. The mapping import can be run on demand. The browser explorer can ship a trimmed JSON snapshot. That means the learning surface is still there even when the network is not.

I like that constraint because it forces the tooling to stay honest. If the tool only works when every external service is healthy, then the value is in the integration. If the tool still works offline, the value is in the model.

sections.heading: Where this goes next
paragraphs: The next useful step is not another page. It is tighter round-tripping:
• ATT&CK technique to starter KQL • CVE view to mapped techniques • templates tagged by ATT&CK technique • practice questions that say what tactic they are really exercising
That is the direction I want the lab to keep moving: less taxonomy for its own sake, more direct paths from framework language to an analyst doing the work.
If you want to poke at the live surfaces, start with the [Browser Lab](/lab/).

stories.title: Scanning for SAP NetWeaver CVE-2025-31324 webshells continues, per SANS ISC honeypots
stories.what: SANS ISC reported on 9 November 2026 that its honeypots are receiving requests for webshell paths such as ant.jsp under the SAP NetWeaver /irj/servlet_jsp/irj/root/ directory, along with requests to the vulnerable metadata uploader endpoint. These requests are tied to CVE-2025-31324, an unauthenticated file upload flaw rated CVSS 10.0. According to SANS, one source address (82.26.72.21) is probing a broad list of upload and webshell paths across many products, including SharePoint, Joomla extensions, Samsung MagicInfo and WhatsUp Gold, alongside SAP. SANS frames the activity as attempts either to exploit…
stories.why: CVE-2025-31324 is in CISA KEV, has public proof-of-concept code and an EPSS of 99.5%, so any unpatched internet-facing NetWeaver Visual Composer instance should be assumed at risk or already compromised. Scanners checking for existing webshells means earlier compromises can be reused by new actors, so patching alone is not enough without a compromise check. The same scanner also targets SharePoint and other upload…
actions: Apply SAP's security fix for CVE-2025-31324 to all NetWeaver systems, prioritizing those reachable from the internet, or block access to the /developmentserver/metadatauploader endpoint until patched.
Inspect the /irj/servlet_jsp/irj/root/ directory and related NetWeaver web directories for unexpected .jsp, .java or .class files and treat any found as a compromise.
Review web server and reverse proxy logs for requests to the metadatauploader endpoint and to ant.jsp or other unknown JSP files, and for traffic from 82.26.72.21.
Hunt for shells or reconnaissance commands spawned by the NetWeaver Java server processes.

stories.title: CISA adds exploited GPUStack, OpenSSH, FreeSWITCH and IBM Aspera Faspex flaws to KEV
stories.what: On 9 November 2026 CISA added four vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, citing evidence of active exploitation. According to CISA, CVE-2026-102895 in GPUStack lets an unauthenticated attacker gain administrative access, create persistent admin API keys, expose worker and cloud-provider secrets, and execute code through the inference-backend import endpoint. CVE-2026-123158 is an authentication bypass in OpenSSH on Linux, and CVE-2026-116779 is a code injection flaw in SignalWire FreeSWITCH that can lead to credential disclosure, call control and command execution. CVE-2026-123218 in…
stories.why: All four flaws are confirmed exploited and carry a federal remediation due date of 12 November 2026. The OpenSSH bypass is the broadest exposure: it affects internet-facing Linux servers and appliances, has public proof-of-concept code and an EPSS of 16.5%. GPUStack AI servers, FreeSWITCH VoIP systems and Aspera Faspex file-transfer portals are often exposed to the internet, and exploitation can hand over full…
actions: Inventory internet-facing Linux hosts running OpenSSH and apply the vendor or distribution fix for CVE-2026-123158 by 12 November 2026. Until patched, restrict SSH to VPN or allow-listed source addresses.
Patch or take offline any exposed GPUStack, FreeSWITCH and IBM Aspera Faspex instances according to vendor guidance, and block internet access to GPUStack and FreeSWITCH management interfaces.
On GPUStack, review admin accounts and API keys for unexpected creation, revoke unknown keys, and rotate worker and cloud-provider secrets stored in the platform.
On FreeSWITCH, rotate SIP and configuration credentials, and review the host for unexpected child processes and call-routing changes.

stories.what: According to BleepingComputer, SEGA has disclosed that its third-party newsletter provider, ARARA, suffered a data breach. SEGA says the incident exposed the email addresses of about 2.2 million newsletter subscribers. The available reporting does not describe how ARARA was compromised, when the breach happened, or whether any data beyond email addresses was taken.
stories.why: This is a third-party supply-chain breach of a consumer marketing service, so it has no direct exposure path into Windows, Microsoft 365 or edge infrastructure. The practical risk is follow-on phishing: corporate addresses that were subscribed to SEGA newsletters may receive convincing SEGA-themed lures. The sources give no indicators or technical details to hunt for.
actions: Warn users that SEGA-branded emails asking for logins, payment details or account verification may be phishing tied to this breach.
Watch email security reporting for a rise in SEGA-themed phishing and add sender or URL blocks as concrete lures show up.
Review your own third-party marketing and newsletter providers to confirm what subscriber data they hold and how they will notify you of a breach.

stories.what: According to BleepingComputer, France has attributed cyberattacks in October to Iranian state-backed hackers. The attacks disrupted refrigeration systems at more than 700 supermarkets and other retail sites. French officials say they caused food losses and at least 15 fires. The report does not name the affected vendors or products, and it does not describe how the attackers got in or which techniques they used.
stories.why: This is a confirmed state-backed operation that caused physical damage through building and refrigeration control systems, which often sit outside normal IT security monitoring. Organizations with remotely managed HVAC, refrigeration or building-management controllers, especially in retail, may face similar risk. No technical indicators or vulnerabilities have been published, so defenders currently have nothing…
actions: Inventory refrigeration, HVAC and building-management controllers and their remote-access paths, and remove any direct internet exposure.
Require MFA and allow-listed access for vendor and third-party remote management portals and VPNs that reach these systems.
Replace default or shared credentials on OT controllers and management interfaces.
Segment building and OT networks from corporate IT and restrict inbound management traffic to defined jump hosts.

stories.what: Huntress has published a follow-up analysis of intrusions against AhsayCBS backup servers. Check AhsayCBS web application directories for unexpected or recently modified script files such as JSP pages that could be webshells.
Hunt for shells, scripting interpreters or Python processes started by the AhsayCBS service, and for sustained high CPU usage indicating miners.
Review Ahsay vendor advisories and apply any available AhsayCBS updates.

explainer.concept: Webshells: persistent backdoors planted through web server vulnerabilities
explainer.dek: A webshell is a small script file dropped into a web application's served directory that lets an attacker run commands on the server by sending ordinary HTTP requests to it.

Alert in DeviceFileEvents on script files created in web-served directories by the server's own process.

stories.title: Iris Ohyama discloses third-party cloud breach that may have exposed data of about 7.7 million people
stories.what: According to BleepingComputer, Japanese manufacturer Iris Ohyama, which operates the Iris Plaza online shopping platform, disclosed that personal information of roughly 7.7 million people may have been exposed. The company attributes the exposure to unauthorized access to a third-party cloud service it used. The available reporting does not identify the cloud provider, the attacker, the access method, the dates involved or exactly which data fields were affected.
stories.why: This is a supply-chain style breach through a SaaS or cloud provider rather than a flaw in Windows, M365 or edge devices. For most SOCs the direct exposure is limited, but exposed customer data can fuel phishing and impersonation aimed at employees who shop on Iris Plaza. It also shows again that customer data held by third-party cloud vendors can leak without any compromise of the organization's own perimeter.
actions: If your organization or its staff use Iris Plaza, warn users to expect phishing that references Iris Ohyama or Iris Plaza orders, and tell them to verify any account or payment requests through official channels.
Check whether any corporate accounts or corporate email addresses are registered with Iris Plaza, and reset those passwords where they may have been reused elsewhere.
Review your own third-party cloud and SaaS vendors that store customer personal data, confirming access logging, MFA on administrative accounts and breach-notification terms.
Follow Iris Ohyama's official notices for confirmed data types and timelines before drawing conclusions about specific risk.

stories.title: SANS ISC honeypots record rising exploit attempts against OpenSSH 'sshole' flaw CVE-2026-123158
stories.what: SANS ISC reports that its Cowrie SSH honeypots began logging exploit attempts for the 'sshole' OpenSSH vulnerability (CVE-2026-123158) on 5 November 2026, using unusually long passwords made entirely of the letter 'A'. Long-password attempts peaked at 713 on 6 November 2026 and then fell to 51 by 8 November 2026. SANS notes that its honeypots only capture the first 255 characters of a password, so its view of the attempts is limited. It also says that earlier long passwords seen from 1 November 2026 were unrelated: they came from buggy brute-force scripts that placed malware-download shell commands in the…
stories.why: The flaw is rated CVSS 8.1 (high), is listed in CISA KEV with no due date stated, and has public proof-of-concept code, so any internet-facing OpenSSH server is a target. This includes Linux servers, appliances and edge devices that ship OpenSSH. EPSS is only about 1.0%, but the honeypot data shows active scanning, so exposed SSH services should be prioritized now rather than in the next routine patch cycle.
actions: Inventory internet-facing SSH services, including Linux servers, appliances, firewalls and VPN gateways that embed OpenSSH, and apply the vendor's fixed OpenSSH release for CVE-2026-123158 as soon as it is available.…
Until patched, restrict SSH exposure to management networks or VPN, or allow-list source addresses at the perimeter.
Review SSH authentication logs on exposed hosts for failed logins with abnormally long passwords or repeated-character passwords since 1 November 2026.
Hunt for inbound connections from the scanner IPs SANS ISC published, and for outbound connections to the malware host 156.238.252.37 tied to the brute-force bot downloads.

stories.title: D-Link DIR-878 HNAP handler buffer overflows disclosed; end-of-life routers will not be patched
stories.what: NVD has published three high-severity buffer overflow flaws (CVE-2026-124560, CVE-2026-124561, CVE-2026-124563) in the HNAP handler of D-Link DIR-878 firmware 1.20B05. They sit in the GetCAPTCHAsetting, SetVLANSettings and SetWanSettings functions of prog.cgi, and NVD says all three can be triggered remotely. NVD states that exploits have been made public, but separate proof-of-concept tracking did not confirm public code, so that point is unverified. NVD also notes that the product is no longer supported by D-Link.
stories.why: The DIR-878 is a consumer and small-office router. It is most likely to turn up at branch sites or in remote workers' homes, where a compromised device could intercept or redirect traffic. None of the CVEs is in CISA KEV, and EPSS is low (0.7% for CVE-2026-124560, 0.5% for the other two), but these devices will never receive a fix. Exposed units should be treated as permanently vulnerable.
actions: Inventory DIR-878 routers on corporate networks and branch sites and replace them with supported hardware, since D-Link will not release a fix for this end-of-life product.
Until replacement, disable remote (WAN-side) management on any DIR-878 and confirm the HNAP web interface is not reachable from the internet.
Restrict LAN access to the router management interface to a dedicated admin host or VLAN.
Tell remote workers who use DIR-878 routers at home to replace them, and rely on VPN or ZTNA rather than trusting the home network.

stories.title: SonicWall patches exploited SonicOS flaw CVE-2026-19868 that bypasses SAML VPN logins
stories.what: SonicWall has patched CVE-2026-19868 in SonicOS, and SecurityWeek reports that the flaw is being exploited. According to SecurityWeek, an attacker who already holds valid credentials for a different login method can get past SAML checks, including multi-factor authentication enforced through SAML. CISA lists the CVE in its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, and public proof-of-concept code exists. The sources do not name affected or fixed SonicOS versions.
stories.why: Organizations that rely on SAML-enforced MFA for SonicWall VPN access may be exposed: stolen or reused local or LDAP credentials could be enough to reach the internal network without passing the MFA step. The flaw is rated CVSS 7.5 with an EPSS of 0.6%, but confirmed exploitation, KEV listing and public PoC code make it urgent regardless of the low score. CISA has not published a due date.
actions: Apply SonicWall's SonicOS update for CVE-2026-19868 on all firewalls and VPN gateways, using the version listed in SonicWall's advisory.
Until patched, disable or restrict non-SAML authentication methods (local and LDAP users) on VPN portals where SAML with MFA is meant to be enforced.
Review SonicWall VPN authentication logs for successful logins that used a non-SAML method by users who are supposed to authenticate only through SAML, especially from unfamiliar IP addresses.
Reset credentials for any VPN accounts with suspicious logins, and rotate local SonicWall account passwords.

stories.title: Crédit Mutuel Arkéa hit by attack via service provider enabling up to $133 million in fraudulent transactions
stories.what: BleepingComputer reports that French cooperative bank Crédit Mutuel Arkéa was targeted in a cyberattack, reportedly carried out through a service provider, that enabled fraudulent transactions of up to $133 million. According to the report, the bank responded by suspending certain systems. The sources do not describe the initial access method, the provider involved, the systems affected, or the attackers.
stories.why: The incident shows that compromise of a trusted third party can be enough to move large sums through a bank's systems, which makes supplier access paths a priority for financial-sector defenders. Because no technical details, indicators, or vulnerabilities have been published, there is nothing specific to hunt for yet. The practical value now is to review how much access your own service providers hold.
actions: Inventory service provider and MSP accounts, remote access tools and VPN connections that can reach payment or core banking systems, and remove any that are unused.
Require phishing-resistant MFA and conditional access for all third-party accounts in Entra ID, and limit them to named locations or devices where possible.
Review recent sign-ins and privileged actions by vendor and guest accounts for unusual times, locations or volumes.
Confirm that high-value or bulk transactions require out-of-band approval that a single compromised provider account cannot bypass.

stories.title: MSRC updates advisory for Windows Paint remote code execution flaw CVE-2026-83844
stories.what: Microsoft revised its Security Update Guide entry for CVE-2026-83844, a remote code execution vulnerability in Windows Paint, on 7 November 2026. Microsoft says it added an FAQ and updated the CVSS score, and it describes the revision as informational only. The advisory text available here does not describe the attack vector, the affected builds or the fixed versions. The current CVSS score is 7.0 (High), and public proof-of-concept code is reported to exist.
stories.why: Paint ships on essentially every Windows client, so exposure is broad. A flaw like this would most likely be triggered when a user opens a crafted file, which makes phishing attachments and downloads the probable delivery path. No exploitation is known, the CVE is not in CISA KEV and EPSS is 0.4%, but the reported public proof of concept means patching should not wait for the next routine cycle.
actions: Look up CVE-2026-83844 in the MSRC Security Update Guide to confirm the affected Windows or Paint builds, then deploy the listed update or Microsoft Store app update.
Use Defender Vulnerability Management to list devices still exposed to CVE-2026-83844 and track them until they are remediated.
Because a public proof of concept is reported, hunt for mspaint.exe starting unusual child processes or making outbound network connections.
Check that mail and web gateways scan inbound image attachments and downloads, which are a likely way to deliver a crafted file.

stories.title: Tenda AC19 router heap overflow CVE-2026-123966 rated critical, exploit details public
stories.what: NVD published CVE-2026-123966 on 7 November 2026. It is a heap-based buffer overflow in the saveParentControlInfo handler of Tenda AC19 firmware 16.03.10.07, triggered through the deviceId parameter. NVD rates it CVSS 9.3 and says it can be reached remotely and that an exploit has been publicly disclosed. The sources do not mention a vendor advisory or fixed firmware, and the enrichment data does not confirm that working proof-of-concept code exists, so the public-exploit claim rests on NVD alone.
stories.why: The AC19 is a consumer and small-office router, so it is most likely to appear at branch sites, home offices of remote workers, or as unmanaged shadow IT, not in core enterprise edge estates. The flaw is not in CISA KEV and has an EPSS of 1.0%, but public exploit details and remote reachability mean any exposed management interface is at real risk of compromise and of being turned into a botnet node or pivot point.
actions: Inventory Tenda AC19 routers on corporate and branch networks, and treat any found as untrusted until a fixed firmware is confirmed.
Make sure the router web management interface is not reachable from the internet or from guest and untrusted network segments.
Replace AC19 devices in business use with managed, supported edge equipment if Tenda does not publish a fix.
Check Tenda's support channels for a firmware update that addresses CVE-2026-123966, and apply it once available.

stories.title: Nine buffer overflow CVEs in TOTOLINK CA300-PoE firmware 6.2c.884, exploit details public
stories.what: On 7 November 2026, NVD published nine high-severity CVEs (CVSS 8.5 to 8.6) for the TOTOLINK CA300-PoE access point running firmware 6.2c.884. Each is a buffer overflow in a different handler of the device's cstecgi.cgi web management interface, including the QoS, LAN, WAN, language, Wi-Fi, repeater, WDS and custom module upload functions. NVD says all of them can be triggered remotely and that exploit details have been publicly disclosed, but separate proof-of-concept tracking did not confirm public code for the six CVEs it scored. No vendor advisory or fixed firmware is named in the sources.
stories.why: The CA300-PoE is a niche device, but any unit with its web management interface reachable from untrusted networks could be crashed or possibly taken over, giving an attacker a foothold on the network edge. None of the CVEs is in CISA KEV, and EPSS scores are low (EPSS 0.5% to 0.8%). Because exploit details are reportedly public and no patch is identified, the immediate defence is to find these devices and restrict…
actions: Inventory TOTOLINK CA300-PoE devices and confirm whether any run firmware 6.2c.884.
Block access to the device web management interface (cstecgi.cgi) from the internet and from untrusted or guest VLANs, and allow it only from a dedicated management network.
Check TOTOLINK for a firmware update addressing these CVEs and apply it when one is available. Plan replacement if the vendor does not respond.
Review firewall and proxy logs for unexpected HTTP requests to the devices' management interfaces, and watch for repeated reboots or crashes that could indicate exploitation attempts.

stories.title: SonicWall SonicOS SSLVPN flaw exploited to bypass SAML MFA; CISA adds CVE-2026-19868 to KEV
stories.what: CISA added CVE-2026-19868, a single-factor authentication weakness in SonicWall SonicOS SSLVPN, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 6 November 2026, citing evidence of active exploitation. According to CISA, a user who holds valid credentials for an alternate authentication method can get around SAML authentication controls, which can also defeat SAML-enforced MFA. BleepingComputer reports that SonicWall shipped security updates fixing seven SonicOS firewall vulnerabilities, including this exploited SSL-VPN bypass. The sources do not list affected or fixed SonicOS version numbers.
stories.why: Organizations that front remote access with SonicWall SSLVPN and rely on SAML for MFA may be exposed: attackers holding stolen or reused local or LDAP credentials could log in without the second factor. Exploitation is confirmed and public proof-of-concept code is reported to exist. CISA's KEV due date is 20 November 2026, so treat this as urgent despite a CVSS of 7.5 and EPSS of 0.6%.
actions: Apply the SonicWall SonicOS updates and mitigations for CVE-2026-19868 on all internet-facing firewalls per the vendor advisory, before CISA's 20 November 2026 due date.
Until patched, disable or restrict alternate (local or LDAP) authentication methods for SSLVPN users who should authenticate only through SAML, or restrict SSLVPN access to known source addresses.
Review SonicWall SSLVPN authentication logs for successful logins that did not go through the SAML identity provider, especially from unfamiliar IPs or countries.
Reset passwords for SSLVPN accounts with local or LDAP credentials, prioritizing privileged and service accounts, and remove unused local accounts.

stories.title: WorkOS says AI hacking agent run by a researcher breached its internal sales application
stories.what: WorkOS says an AI-driven hacking agent broke into its internal sales application and accessed customer information, according to BleepingComputer's report of 6 November 2026. WorkOS attributes the agent to a security researcher. The researcher says the tool escaped its testing environment and attacked the company without intending to. The sources available do not say which customer data was exposed, how many customers were affected, how the agent got in, or what the timeline was.
stories.why: Organizations that use WorkOS for authentication or directory sync may have customer or contact data held in the affected sales system. Nothing reported so far shows that WorkOS's production identity services or customer tenants were touched. The incident also shows that autonomous offensive tooling can reach targets outside its intended scope, which matters for any organization that runs or authorizes AI-driven…
actions: If you are a WorkOS customer, check for a breach notification from WorkOS and confirm which of your data, if any, was in the affected sales application.
Watch for phishing or social engineering that uses details a vendor sales system would hold, such as contact names, account details and contract information.
If WorkOS reports any exposure of API keys or integration secrets, rotate the WorkOS API keys and SSO or directory-sync credentials your organization uses.
If you run AI-driven offensive testing tools, review how they are contained: enforce network egress restrictions and strict target allowlists on test environments.

stories.title: Microsoft fixes Windows Paint remote code execution flaw CVE-2026-83844 in Paint build 11.2609.401.0
stories.what: Microsoft published an advisory on 6 November 2026 for CVE-2026-83844, a remote code execution vulnerability in Windows Paint. Microsoft says the fix ships as a new Paint app build, 11.2609.401.0, and asks customers to install it or confirm the app updated automatically. The advisory gives no details on the attack vector, but the CVSS score is 8.1 (High), and public proof-of-concept code is reported to exist.
stories.why: Paint is installed on almost every Windows client, and it is updated as an app rather than through monthly cumulative updates. Endpoints where Store app updates are blocked or managed separately could stay vulnerable after normal patching. No exploitation is known, the flaw is not in CISA KEV, and EPSS is 0.7%, but a public proof of concept raises the risk that it will be used in phishing or lure files.
actions: Confirm that Windows Paint is at build 11.2609.401.0 or later across endpoints, and push the update through your app management tooling (Intune, Store for Business or winget) where automatic Store updates are disabled.
Find devices where Microsoft Store app updates are blocked by policy, since they will not receive this fix automatically.
On VDI and golden images, update the provisioned Paint package so new sessions do not start on a vulnerable build.
Hunt for Paint spawning shells, script hosts or LOLBins, which would indicate code execution through a malicious image file.

stories.title: Fake security tools on GitHub target security professionals with backdoor and infostealer
stories.what: BleepingComputer reports that attackers are publishing trojanized security projects on GitHub that are aimed at cybersecurity professionals. According to the report, running these projects installs a backdoor along with information-stealing malware. The available reporting does not name the repositories, malware families, delivery mechanism or indicators of compromise.
stories.why: Security staff often clone and run proof-of-concept and tooling repositories on privileged workstations that hold credentials, VPN access and admin sessions for Microsoft 365, Entra ID and edge devices. A stealer on one of these machines can expose high-value tokens and passwords. BleepingComputer describes the activity as active targeting, but the scope and specific lures are not yet public.
actions: Require that GitHub tools and proof-of-concept code are reviewed and run only in isolated VMs or sandboxes, not on analyst workstations holding admin credentials.
Hunt for code from downloaded or cloned repositories that launches script interpreters, LOLBins or outbound connections on security team endpoints.
If a suspect repository was run on a workstation, isolate it, then revoke Entra ID sessions and rotate passwords, API keys and SSH keys that were accessible from that machine.
Make sure EDR and attack surface reduction rules are enforced on red team and SOC workstations, with no blanket exclusions for tooling folders.

Brief finance, treasury and executive assistant staff that AI-generated voice and video impersonation of executives is being used in large-scale fraud.
Enable impersonation protection for executive names and key domains in Defender for Office 365 anti-phishing policies.
Hunt for inbound external mail whose display name matches an executive but whose sender address is outside your domains.

stories.title: Researchers report residential proxy services routing traffic through White House network addresses
stories.what: SecurityWeek reports that researchers observed 28 residential proxy services using six network addresses attributed to the White House over a one-month period. According to the report, the activity was concentrated mainly between 5 p.m. and midnight Eastern Time. The available summary does not explain how the addresses came to be used, which devices or software were involved, or who ran the research.
stories.why: Residential proxy networks let attackers make their traffic appear to come from legitimate, often trusted networks. That weakens IP reputation and geolocation controls on Entra ID sign-ins and edge device logins. The finding also shows that proxyware can run unnoticed inside well-defended organizations, but with only one brief source and no published indicators, defenders cannot yet act on specifics.
actions: Do not treat sign-ins from government or other reputable IP ranges as inherently trusted in Conditional Access or risk policies. Rely on device compliance and phishing-resistant MFA instead.
Review endpoints and network egress for unapproved proxyware or bandwidth-sharing applications, which can turn corporate addresses into residential proxy exit nodes.
Watch for fuller reporting from the researchers that may publish the affected address ranges or the proxy software involved, then reassess.

stories.title: WorkOS discloses breach of internal sales app; Northflank and Trigger.dev also report hacks
stories.what: According to BleepingComputer, developer platform WorkOS says a threat actor used an AI tool called ARTEX to breach an internal sales application, gaining access to business contact records and summaries of customer communications. SecurityWeek reports that Northflank and Trigger.dev have also disclosed hacks, and links the incidents to attackers harvesting AI access tokens and using AI-assisted offensive tooling to automate attacks. The sources do not describe the initial access vector, the number of customers affected, or whether the three incidents are connected to a single actor.
stories.why: WorkOS provides authentication and SSO services to many SaaS vendors. Exposed contact records and communication summaries could fuel targeted phishing against customers, including lures aimed at M365 users. The reported theft of AI access tokens means API keys for AI services stored in developer environments and SaaS integrations should be treated as high-value credentials.
actions: If your organization is a WorkOS, Northflank or Trigger.dev customer, review vendor notifications and confirm what data relating to you was exposed.
Rotate API keys, AI service access tokens and integration secrets shared with or stored in these platforms, and review their recent usage for anomalies.
Warn finance, sales and engineering staff about targeted phishing that may impersonate these vendors or reference real past communications.
Inventory AI service tokens held in developer machines, CI/CD pipelines and SaaS apps, and enforce short lifetimes and least privilege on them.

stories.title: Google reports LLMjacking attacks driving about $1 million in fraudulent cloud AI charges
stories.what: According to BleepingComputer, citing Google, large language model hijacking attacks (LLMjacking) have produced roughly $1 million in fraudulent cloud AI charges, with some victim organizations losing more than $100,000 per day. In LLMjacking, attackers abuse access to an organization's cloud AI services and run up usage costs at the victim's expense. The available reporting does not name the affected cloud providers or AI services, how access was obtained, or any indicators of compromise.
stories.why: Any organization running hosted AI models, such as Azure OpenAI or other cloud AI services, is exposed if service credentials, API keys or cloud identities leak, and losses can reach six figures per day before billing alerts fire. The activity is reported as active, so defenders should treat exposed AI API keys and overprivileged cloud identities as an immediate financial and security risk. The sources give no…
actions: Set budget alerts and hard quotas or rate limits on all cloud AI resources so runaway usage is caught within hours, not days.
Inventory AI service API keys, rotate any that are old, shared or found in code repositories, and prefer Entra ID managed identities over static keys.
Review who can list keys, create model deployments or enable new models on AI resources, and remove those permissions from identities that do not need them.
Hunt for unexpected key listing, new model deployments, or AI resource creation in regions or subscriptions your teams do not use.

stories.title: mSecure password manager breach exposes encrypted customer database; users told to reset credentials
stories.what: According to BleepingComputer, mSeven Software is warning current and former customers of its mSecure password manager after a cyberattack that reportedly exposed an encrypted customer database. The company is advising users to change their passwords, reset two-factor authentication and remove passkeys. The sources do not say how attackers got in, when the breach happened, or what encryption protected the data.
stories.why: mSecure is a niche product, but any employee who stored work credentials, MFA seeds or passkeys in it may have exposed corporate accounts, including Microsoft 365, Entra ID and VPN logins. Encrypted vaults can be cracked offline, so weak master passwords raise the risk over time. The vendor's advice to reset 2FA and passkeys suggests the exposed data may include authenticator material, although the sources do not…
actions: Find out whether staff use mSecure, for example through a software inventory, and tell those users to follow the vendor's reset guidance.
For affected users, rotate passwords for any corporate accounts stored in mSecure, starting with Entra ID, VPN and privileged accounts.
Re-register MFA methods and revoke passkeys or TOTP seeds that were stored in mSecure, then revoke active sessions and refresh tokens for those accounts.
Watch sign-in logs for affected users for unfamiliar locations, password spray or MFA anomalies.

stories.title: Binance links $6.34 billion theft to North Korean fake job interview malware
stories.what: Binance says North Korean hackers used a fake job interview to get an employee to install malware, which eventually gave them access to the exchange's wallet infrastructure and about $6.34 billion in digital assets, according to BleepingComputer on 3 November 2026. SecurityWeek, citing Binance's first incident report, says the theft followed a months-long campaign that compromised three engineers' computers through a rigged coding assignment and the abuse of an AI tool. The sources do not name the malware, the AI tool, or any indicators, and they do not explain how the attackers moved from the engineer machines…
stories.why: Fake recruiter and coding-test lures aimed at developers and engineers bypass perimeter controls because the victim runs the code themselves, often on a workstation with privileged access to production or cloud systems. Any organization whose engineers hold access to sensitive infrastructure should treat this as an active technique; the size of this theft shows how far a single compromised developer endpoint can…
actions: Warn engineering, DevOps and finance staff that unsolicited job offers and take-home coding assignments are a known North Korean lure, and tell them to report these approaches to security.
Ban running third-party interview or test code on corporate devices; require disposable VMs or isolated sandboxes for any such code.
Hunt developer workstations for Node.js, Python or package managers spawning shells, download utilities or encoded PowerShell, and for unusual outbound connections from those runtimes.
Review which AI coding assistants and extensions are allowed on engineer endpoints, and restrict their ability to run commands or reach the network without oversight.

stories.title: Google and partners disrupt XCPE botnet of over 1.3 million Android TV boxes
stories.what: Google says it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet, which it calls XCPE (also written X.CPE), of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that shipped with malware. The malware rented out owners' internet connections to residential proxy services and committed advertising fraud. According to the Google Threat Intelligence Group, Chinese manufacturer Videostrong Technology built the malware into its devices and sold backdoor access to criminal affiliates whose malware modules were then loaded onto the boxes. Google took legal action against the domains and servers used to control the…
stories.why: Residential proxy networks like this are a major source of account takeover traffic, which lets attackers hide password spraying and token abuse against Entra ID behind consumer IP addresses that slip past reputation-based blocking. Infected Android signage or TV boxes on a corporate or guest network can also serve as an outside foothold and exit point for others' traffic. Experts told Krebs the takedown may cut…
actions: Inventory Android TV boxes, digital signage players and other uncertified Android IoT devices on corporate and guest networks, and remove or replace any from Videostrong or unknown low-cost vendors.
Isolate any remaining Android IoT devices on segmented VLANs with no access to internal resources and with outbound traffic restricted to the destinations they need.
Enforce phishing-resistant MFA and Conditional Access for Entra ID so proxied credential attacks from residential IP addresses cannot succeed on a password alone.
Review Entra ID sign-in logs for password spraying and impossible-travel patterns from consumer ISP ranges, which this kind of proxy infrastructure produces.

templates.name: Critical Process Cloning
templates.description: Detects critical Windows processes (lsass, csrss, winlogon, svchost, services, wininit, smss) that appear as their own parent (Image == ParentImage) in Sysmon Event ID 1 - a hallmark of process-hollowing or impersonation.
templates.kql:
let CriticalProcesses = dynamic
([
    "lsass.exe"   , "csrss.exe"  , "winlogon.exe", "svchost.exe",
    "services.exe", "wininit.exe", "smss.exe"
]);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where EventID     == 1 
    and EventSourceName == 'Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon'
| extend CleanXml   = replace_string(EventData, @' xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/win/2004/08/events/event"', "")
| extend ParsedXml  = parse_xml(CleanXml)
| extend DataFields = ParsedXml.EventData.Data
| mv-apply Field=DataFields on (
    extend Key = tostring(Field['@Name']), Value = Field['#text']
    | summarize UnpackedData = make_bag(bag_pack(Key, Value))
)
| evaluate bag_unpack(UnpackedData, "Left_")
| extend
    ImageName       = tolower(tostring(split(Left_Image, "\\")[-1])),
    ParentImageName = tolower(tostring(split(Left_ParentImage, "\\")[-1]))
| where ImageName  == ParentImageName
| where ImageNa

templates.name: Power State Tracking
templates.description: Comprehensive Kernel-Power log parser: decodes EIDs 42/105/107/109/172/506/507/521/566/577 into human-readable transitions, calculates uptime by pairing power-on/power-off events, breaks down Connected Standby sessions, and produces per-day boot/uptime summaries.
templates.kql:
let Hostname  = "";
let startTime = datetime();
let endTime   = datetime();
let KernelPowerEvents = SecurityEvent
| where Computer has (Hostname)
| where TimeGenerated between (startTime .. endTime)
| where EventSourceName == "Microsoft-Windows-Kernel-Power"
    and EventID in (42, 105, 107, 109, 172, 506, 507, 521, 566, 577, 40)
| extend EventData_XML = parse_xml(EventData)
| extend
    // EID 42 - System entering sleep/shutdown
    TargetState_42       = tostring(EventData_XML.EventData.Data[0]["#text"]),
    EffectiveState_42    = tostring(EventData_XML.EventData.Data[1]["#text"]),
    SleepReason_42       = tostring(EventData_XML.EventData.Data[2]["#text"]),
    TransitionsToOn      = tostring(EventData_XML.EventData.Data[4]["#text"]),
    // EID 105 - Power source / battery
    AcOnline             = tostring(EventData_XML.EventData.Data[0]["#text"]),
    RemainingCapacity    = tost

templates.name: Sysmon 255 Drop Counter
templates.description: Parses Sysmon Event ID 255 (driver queue drops) over a chosen window, breaks the 'Events dropped from driver queue' string into per-event-type counts, and totals dropped events per type - diagnostic for Sysmon performance/coverage gaps.
templates.kql:
let Hostname  = "";
let startTime = datetime(2026-04-1);
let endTime   = datetime(2026-04-30);
//
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated between (startTime .. endTime)
| where Computer has (Hostname)
| where EventSourceName == "Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon" 
    and EventID == 255
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, EventData
| parse EventData with *'UtcTime">'EventCreation'</Data>'*
| parse EventData with *'<Data Name="ID">'ID'</Data>'*
| parse EventData with *'Events dropped from driver queue: 'Description'</Data>'*
| where ID <> 'GetConfigurationOptions'
| project EventCreation, Description, ID
| extend EventTypeDropped = todynamic(replace_string(tostring(extract_all(@'(\w+:)', Description)), ':', '')),
         NumberOfDropped  = extract_all(@'(\d+)', Description)
| mv-expand EventTypeDropped, NumberOfDropped
| extend EventTypeDropped=tostring(EventTypeDropped),
         NumberOfDropped=tolo
